transcript.message: Hi, first time buying. Not sure what I should look at first tbh.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.message: Totally normal—there’s a lot to take in for a first purchase. Start by working out whether it’s for your own stay or as an investment, then what budget feels comfortable. From there, you can narrow down location and the features that matter to you. Are you mainly looking for a place to live in yourself, or still figuring that out?

transcript.speaker: customer
transcript.message: Probably for my own stay in a year or two, but I’m not completely sure yet. Budget is the part I’m lost on—how do I work out what monthly payment would be comfortable?

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.message: A good starting point is what you can comfortably manage after essentials, existing debts and regular savings—not the maximum a bank might lend. Include the loan instalment and ongoing costs; for Pearl’s 900 sq ft Type A, maintenance including sinking fund is about RM162 a month, before utilities and other expenses. If you’re comfortable sharing rough take-home income and monthly debt payments, I can help you sketch a budget. No exact details needed.

transcript.speaker: customer
transcript.message: Thanks, that maintenance figure helps. I’d rather not share my income just yet—could you give me a simple rough way to estimate a comfortable monthly instalment?

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.message: A simple rough guide is to keep total housing costs around 25–30% of your take-home pay. That’s for everything monthly, not just the loan: subtract Pearl’s roughly RM162 maintenance for a 900 sq ft unit, plus an allowance for utilities and other ongoing costs, to get a rough instalment ceiling. If you have other debts or want more breathing room, aim lower. It’s just a budgeting guide, not a bank’s approval limit.

transcript.speaker: customer
transcript.message: Hi, first time buying. Not sure what I should look at first tbh.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.message: Hi! Totally normal for a first purchase. A good place to start is: decide whether it’s for your own stay or investment, set a comfortable overall budget including upfront and ongoing costs, and shortlist areas that suit your needs. Then compare the actual layout and ownership costs—not just the headline price. Are you mainly looking for a place to live in, or an investment?

transcript.speaker: customer
transcript.message: Probably own stay in 1–2 years, but I’m not completely sure yet. I’m a bit worried about financing—should I work out a comfortable monthly payment first before looking at places?

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.message: Yes—working backwards from a monthly payment that feels comfortable is a sensible first step before narrowing down places. Leave room for upfront costs and ongoing ownership costs too, and treat a bank’s maximum loan as a ceiling, not your target. What monthly range would feel manageable for you?

transcript.speaker: customer
transcript.message: I haven’t figured out a range yet. How do I estimate a comfortable monthly amount without knowing what I can borrow?

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.message: You don’t need to know your borrowing limit yet. Use your take-home pay and look at a few recent months of spending: subtract regular bills, debt payments, savings you want to keep putting aside, and a buffer for unexpected costs. What’s left can help you choose a provisional monthly housing budget—but don’t assume it should all go to the loan payment. Remember to allow for other ownership costs too, like maintenance, utilities and insurance. It’s a starting point, not a loan assessment. If you’re comfortable, you can share your rough take-home pay and monthly commitments, and we can work out a first estimate.

transcript.speaker: customer
transcript.message: That makes sense. I’m not quite comfortable sharing my pay details yet—could you show me a simple example of how to work it out?

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.message: Sure—just a made-up example, not a borrowing estimate. If take-home pay were RM5,000: subtract RM1,500 for regular bills, RM500 for debt payments, RM800 you want to save, and RM500 as a buffer. That leaves RM1,700 for housing costs altogether. If you set aside, say, RM400 for things like maintenance, utilities and insurance, you’d have about RM1,300 left as a possible loan-payment budget. The amounts will vary, and upfront costs need planning separately. You can try the same calculation privately with your own numbers—no need to share them here.

transcript.speaker: customer
transcript.message: Thanks, that example makes it much clearer. I’ll try it with my own numbers. What upfront costs should I start planning for separately?

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.message:
Good question. It helps to plan for a few separate buckets:

• Booking/earnest deposit and the balance of your down payment, depending on the loan amount and sale terms. The deposit is often credited toward the purchase price, but check the terms.
• Legal fees and stamp duty for the purchase, plus legal fees and stamp duty for the loan.
• Possible loan-related costs, such as valuation, and insurance or takaful if applicable.
• Moving and setup costs, including utility deposits, basic furnishings or repairs.

The amounts depend on the property price, financing and current rules, so there isn’t a reliable total to quote yet. A solicitor and bank can confirm the applicable fees once you have a specific property and loan in mind.

transcript.speaker: customer
transcript.message: Thanks, that gives me a clearer picture. I’ll work out my monthly comfort range and see what I can set aside for upfront costs first. After that, is it worth doing a basic bank check before I start viewing places?

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.message: Yes, an initial bank affordability check can be useful before you view—it may give you a rough guide to what you could borrow. The bank may ask about your income, employment and existing commitments, and what documents it needs varies. Treat any early estimate as indicative, not loan approval or a guaranteed amount; a formal application involves fuller checks. You can ask the bank whether it’s just an initial review or a formal application, and whether it includes a credit-record enquiry. No need to share your figures here.

transcript.speaker: customer
transcript.message: Thanks, that’s helpful. I’ll work out my own numbers first, then ask a bank what kind of check they’re doing. If I speak to a few banks, could that lead to multiple credit-record enquiries?

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.message: I’ve registered that for verification. I don’t have the confirmed answer yet.

transcript.speaker: customer
transcript.message: Okay, thanks for checking. I’ll wait for the confirmed answer before speaking to a few banks.
